summary:
This L0009 run, from 06:29 UTC on Nov 26, was started by the line's timer, not by an instruction. It had no 'Asked' items, so the empty answers list is right. It made no claims. It traced the overlap error that stopped the seed 1, f* 0.3 stall layer in E0104 and fixed it on branch method/rest (83532c8, decision D0089). It reran the three 2D stall layers as E0105 and recorded that experiment as falsified. The fix and the falsification both stand. One headline sentence goes past the evidence, the numbers behind the question to Chris are inflated by the loop itself, and the experiment was registered after its results existed.

What reproduces. In a scratch clone of 83532c8 I ran the session's own command (feed_run.py, loop limit 30) for seed 1 and seed 2 at f* 0.3. Apart from CPU times, both result files match the session's in every field: stack counts, engine counters, stop reason, stop time, hit speeds and lifetimes. Seed 1 stops in a same-instant loop at t = 5.870650988602072: the touch 84-93 builds a stack, the touch 93-94 asks to join, and the start is refused. Seed 2 stops with 'sphere penetrates the bottom plate' after the step to 6.22, with 19,779 fallback collisions. The fix acted: the largest hand-back snap is 5e-15 at seed 1 and 5e-12 at seed 2, against 3.2e-6 before. Neither run gained energy at any touch, and the engine's gain counter is zero. I also ran E0104's code (c6dfd4d) on seed 2 with per-call tracing. It loops at t = 6.242660634071709 (pairs 54-60 and 60-67, about 2.3 s of CPU per round), as the diagnosis says. So the line state's sentence that both other layers looped at one instant under the old code now holds for both. Last review confirmed the f* 0.4 loop. The five recorded files in runs/E0105 match their SHA-256.

What is wrong.
(1) The headline says 'Each now stops in a same-instant loop, or, for seed 2, on a sphere penetrating the plate.' That is not known for the seed 1, f* 0.4 layer, and my trace says it is not a loop. I reran that layer on 83532c8 for nine minutes and logged every stack handler call. It reproduces the session's log to 5.25 (19 built, 17 broken). Then simulated time keeps advancing, but very slowly. The last calls fall at 5.25079, 5.25108, 5.25169 and 5.25175, with 30 to 70 seconds of CPU between them. That is roughly 70 seconds for 6e-5 time units, with half a time unit left to finish the cycle. The pattern is a slow crawl through stack integration, the old stall in a new form, not a same-instant loop. The session's own job log has not moved past 5.25 since 07:03. The loop detector only fires on calls at one exact event time, and feed_run.py checks its CPU cap only between 0.01 steps, the same flaw I raised about feed_capped.py last review. So this job will probably run to its 3-hour wall-clock timeout, about 10:00 UTC, not the 08:10 that active.jsonl gives. The timer run that collects it should expect no result file, only a timeout. I could not see the session's process from my sandbox, so I can't confirm it is still alive.
(2) The question to Chris says '38 touches hit stack spheres. 18 were at or above the rest speed ... 17 of the 18 breaks would have been bounces.' Fifteen of those 38 'touches' are the seed 1 loop's own touch, 93-94 at zero approach speed, repeated at t = 5.8707. There were 23 real touches, 18 of them (78%) at or above the rest speed, with a median approach speed of 0.017, not the recorded 0.0095. Likewise, 15 of the 37 recorded stack lifetimes are zero-length loop stacks. Without them the median lifetime is 0.00047, not the recorded 8.2e-5. The '35 built, 34 broken' counts include the same 15 repeats. The bounce question also omits seed 2. There, 9 of 13 touches broke a stack, and 5 of those 9 came above the wake speed. So the bounce rule would have saved only 4 of the 9 stacks there. Chris should see both layers.
(3) Pre-registration came after the results. The E0105 registration is stamped 07:05. Its runs started at 07:00:48 (active.jsonl), its artifact A0199 was created at 07:00:52, and its seed 1 and seed 2 result files were written at 07:03 and 07:04. All of it was committed at 07:10:45 together with the outcome. Its method text also cites a trace result (5.8916). Under the program's rules this registration doesn't count as made before the run.
(4) Several timestamps are not measured. The line note is stamped 07:12 and the line update 07:13, and the summary's 'ended' is 07:11:30, but the commits holding them were made at 07:10:45 and 07:10:50.

Smaller points. A0199 is recorded with 0 bytes (three empty logs). The evidence cites the two finished result files, which are not in any artifact manifest yet. program check warns that A0199 changed. Re-recording it when f* 0.4 is collected fixes this. active.jsonl still lists pids 1075 and 1078, whose runs ended and were collected this session. The line state's 'spheres handed back move by round-off only (5e-15)' quotes seed 1 only; seed 2's largest snap is 5e-12, still tiny. The progress file's 'Older state' still says E0104 reached 5.88; it reached 5.89.

Last review's points. The misleading 'no reported progress' sentence is gone from the line state. The CPU budget figure is now right: 291.2 is program check's 290.5 plus this run's 0.7. D0089 takes up my point that the old join treated the stack as immovable. My point that the CPU cap is only checked between steps was not addressed, and it is why (1) will cost about three hours of CPU.

Line state for L0009. Each sentence holds except where it says or implies that every layer now stops in a loop or a penetration. The state itself says only that f* 0.4 was looping under E0104's code, which is correct. Only the summary's headline overstates. The 'next' item 'Collect ... seed 1 f* 0.4 run' should expect a timeout, not a result.

Housekeeping. program check passes now. During the review it failed only on my own scratch folder, which I removed. It also warned that A0199 had changed. The latest approval is approved/20261124T031934, more than a day old. The data folder is 693 megabytes of the 15 gigabyte limit, with 82 gigabytes free against a floor of 40. tmp/ is empty. Nothing was written outside the program's folders in the run's window.

run_conditions.assessment: The run started at 06:29:08, eight seconds after its scheduled time. It finished within its hour: the last commit was at 07:10:50. Most of its work landed: a traced cause, a code fix, two finished reruns and a diagnosis of the old loops. The f* 0.4 layer was left running. That job is not waiting on the machine but crawling inside one step that its own CPU cap cannot interrupt. The machine did not limit the science: load was about 6.6 on 40 cores when I checked, and disk and data size are well inside budget. The 10-minute interruption was a wait on the run's own traced reruns, not a stall of the machine. pmset, ps and uptime are absent on this Linux worker, so I could not check sleep or the session's processes. The recorded 0.7 CPU-hours is plausible: the two finished runs used 144 and 82 seconds.
discrepancies: The summary's 'ended' (07:11:30) and the line note and update (stamped 07:12 and 07:13) are later than the commits that contain them (07:10:45 and 07:10:50).

active.jsonl gives 08:10 as the expected finish of the f* 0.4 job. Its log has not advanced since 07:03, and my rerun of the same code crawls at about 70 s of CPU per 6e-5 time units past 5.2508. The CPU cap is checked only between steps, so the job will likely run to its 3-hour timeout, about 10:00.
active.jsonl still lists the seed 1 and seed 2 f* 0.3 processes (pids 1075 and 1078), which finished at 07:03 and 07:04 and were collected this session.
Artifact A0199 is recorded as three empty files (0 bytes). It now holds five files, 147 kB, and the evidence cites two result files that no manifest records.
